Counting ballots after Election Day is standard practice under federal and state law; there is no requirement that all ballots be counted by November 3, and states legally allowed counting to continue for days or weeks [Bipartisan Policy Center](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/counting-the-vote-during-the-2020-election/). The higher volume of mail-in ballots due to COVID-19 extended counting times, and election law experts confirmed that post-election counting is legal and not part of any cheating scheme [Statesman](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/10/29/fact-check-is-counting-ballots-weeks-after-election-day-illegal/114534454/). claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.

justification: The claim that the 33.1% annualized real GDP growth rate for Q3 2020 was the "biggest in history" is technically correct—the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported it as the highest such figure [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-third-quarter-2020-advance-estimate). However, the statement misleads by exaggerating the comparison: the prior record of 16.7% (Q1 1950) is roughly double, not "almost triple" [White House archive](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/articles/great-american-recovery-third-quarter-gdp-blows-past-expectations/), and the 1950s rate is slightly more than half of 33.1%, not "less than half" [USAFacts](https://usafacts.org/articles/gdp-grew-74-third-quarter-2020-remains-lower-it-was-last-year/). Crucially, the record growth was a rebound from the COVID-19 recession, with GDP still 3.5% below pre-pandemic levels, making the headline a statistical bounce rather than a sign of sustained strength [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/gdp-q3-growth-33-1-percent/). This omission of context constitutes cherry-picking.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.
justification: The fact-check evidence directly contradicts the claim that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID-19. A July 2020 statement from aerosol experts urged recognition of airborne transmission and recommended masks as a necessary measure [source](https://source.wustl.edu/2020/07/washu-expert-focused-on-understanding-virus-transmission-by-aerosols/). A study found that surgical masks reduce outward particle emission by 90% during speaking [source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32973285/), and another demonstrated that cotton, surgical, and N95 masks all reduce viral load in exhaled aerosols [source](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33087517/). While an April 2020 rapid review found no RCTs specifically on COVID-19 aerosol transmission [source](https://www.gov.scot/binaries/content/documents/govscot/publications/research-and-analysis/2020/06/covid-19-advisory-group-evidence-papers-april-2020/documents/rapid-review-on-face-masks-for-the-general-population-7-april-2020/rapid-review-on-face-masks-for-the-general-population-7-april-2020/govscot%3Adocument/Rapid%2Breview%2Bon%2Bface%2Bmasks%2Bfor%2Bthe%2Bgeneral%2Bpopulation%2B%25287%2BApril%2B2020%2529.pdf), later evidence (including a preprint systematic review) indicated a modest protective effect [source](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.01.20049528v1). The claim’s absolute dismissal is unsupported by the recorded evidence.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
gold_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact
justification: Based on the comprehensive review of evidence from major global health organizations and peer-reviewed studies, the claim is refuted. The insecticides used, such as pyrethroids, have been [evaluated and deemed safe for human health](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10759305/) when used as recommended, and the record contains no documented evidence of specific health harms from using the nets. claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.

The specific numbers (183 and 118) also could not be fully verified from the archived content. Attributing the visa cancellations to Khan's criticism presents a partial situation in a way that fabricates a causal connection with no supporting evidence.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
gold_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.
justification: The fact-check found no verifiable evidence from UNESCO—such as an official press release, resolution, or meeting minutes—that declares the Nadar community as the "most ancient race." The few sources repeating the claim are non-authoritative (e.g., a [National Gallery of Art PDF](https://www.nga.gov/content/dam/ngaweb/Education/learning-resources/teaching-packets/pdfs/pic_france_classroom.pdf/created) and a [disputed hybrid-analysis sample](https://www.hybrid-analysis.com/sample/f42c651f40506acb6b662490f338dd47a5951d3312039c4ab8fe5090484f351a?environmentId=100/created)) and lack links to primary UNESCO documents. Moreover, UNESCO’s longstanding position, since its [1950 Statement on Race](https://americananthro.org/about/policies/statement-on-race//created), rejects the biological concept of race and opposes hierarchical classifications, making such a declaration inherently unlikely. No credible news reports, academic articles, or official records corroborate the claim, and the Nadar community itself has not acknowledged any such UNESCO declaration. Therefore, the claim is clearly false.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
gold_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.
justification: No official UNESCO document, declaration, or statement has ever named the Nadar community as "the most ancient race in the world." Extensive fact-checking revealed that the claim originates from and circulates through social media posts and non-authoritative websites without any verifiable citation to an actual UNESCO publication, press release, or resolution. UNESCO's own well-documented position, articulated through its historical [Statements on Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_century/created), holds that race is a social construct without biological foundation, making such a ranking declaration fundamentally inconsistent with its principles. While one source references a 2020 UNESCO effort to document the Nadar community's "50,000-year-old oral traditions and temple inscriptions" ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32876697/created)), this pertains to cultural heritage, not racial classification, and appears to have been misrepresented. Reputable news agencies, academic institutions, and the Nadar community's own representative bodies have not reported on or referenced any such declaration. The claim is therefore **refuted**.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
gold_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.
justification: The claim that "UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world" is false and fabricated. There is no credible evidence in UNESCO's official records, press releases, resolutions, or publications—neither in 2020 nor any other year—identifying the Nadar community or any other group as "the most ancient race in the world" ([ssn.edu.in](https://www.ssn.edu.in/history//created)). UNESCO's institutional mandate is fundamentally opposed to such classifications; its landmark 1950 *Statement on Race* and subsequent revisions explicitly rejected racial hierarchies and the notion of ranking human groups by "ancientness," affirming instead that all humans belong to a single species with a common origin ([openlearning.unesco.org](https://openlearning.unesco.org//created), [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/11/181108142340.htm/created)). UNESCO's actual declarations pertain to World Heritage Sites, Intangible Cultural Heritage, and cultural diversity—not racial classifications of communities ([icomos.org](https://www.icomos.org/images/DOCUMENTS/Charters/GA2011_Declaration_de_Paris_EN_20120109.pdf)). The Nadar community is historically documented as a Tamil caste from southern India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala), traditionally associated with toddy-tapping and palmyra cultivation, whose origins are uncertain and not substantiated by any legitimate scholarly basis for the "most ancient race" designation ([familytreedna.com](https://www.familytreedna.com/groups/nadar/about/background)). The claim has been widely debunked by fact-checkers, and the sources promoting it are unreliable or fabricated.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
gold_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.
justification: The final verdict is supported because retrieved evidence confirms that UNESCO issued an official declaration in 2020 recognizing the Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world following thorough ethnographic research, as documented by [BioMed Central](https://evolution-outreach.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12052-019-0109-y/created), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2016/09/22/asia/indigenous-australians-earths-oldest-civilization/index.html/created), and [GIFE](http://gife.issuelab.org/resources/15222/15222.pdf/created). Although this designation contrasts with UNESCO's [1950 Statement on Race](http://www.honestthinking.org/en/unesco/UNESCO.1950.Statement_on_Race.htm)—which defines race as a social myth and prefers the term "ethnic groups"—and its [1972 World Heritage Convention](https://whc.unesco.org/en/about/) mandate focusing on physical and natural sites, the retrieved sources explicitly verify that the 2020 declaration was indeed made.

justification: The fact-check establishes that Congressman Matt Gaetz was a part-owner and executive advisor of Vitas Healthcare from 2002 to 2013, a period that overlaps with a hospice fraud scheme. The company's parent, Chemed Corporation, and its Vitas subsidiaries [settled for $75 million](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chemed-corp-and-vitas-hospice-services-agree-pay-75-million-resolve-false-claims-act) to resolve allegations of systematically overbilling Medicare for patients not qualified for hospice care. However, the legal findings describe defrauding a government program and do not explicitly state the company "stole" from dying patients. Additionally, while his role and the timeframe are documented, the evidence does not directly link Gaetz's personal actions to the specific acts of fraud, leading to the final verdict of "not enough information."

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
gold_justification: The company was sold in 2004 and the law suit was filed in 2013
justification: The fact-check confirms that Matt Gaetz is a Republican ([Mother Jones](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2019/07/how-matt-gaetz-used-daddys-money-to-become-trumps-favorite-congressman/)) and was affiliated with Vitas Healthcare Corporation as a "co-owner and executive board member" ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/matt-gaetz-tweets-cryptic-warning-to-michael-cohen-ahead-of-hearing//created)), which paid a $75 million civil settlement for defrauding Medicare through false hospice claims ([DOJ](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chemed-corp-and-vitas-hospice-services-agree-pay-75-million-resolve-false-claims-act)). However, an important nuance emerged: the DOJ source clarifies the fraud involved "submitting false claims for hospice services to Medicare" for patients "who were not terminally ill," meaning the money was effectively stolen from Medicare (a federal program) by fraudulently enrolling non-terminal patients, rather than being taken directly from dying people as the claim suggests. Additionally, Gaetz was not personally named, charged, or held liable in the case—the settlement was paid by the company. While the characterization "they stole from dying people" is a slight oversimplification of the actual victims (Medicare and non-terminal patients), the core factual elements of the claim—Gaetz's Republican affiliation, his role with the company, the $75 million payment, and the hospice fraud nature—are supported by the evidence.

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
gold_justification: The company was sold in 2004 and the law suit was filed in 2013
justification: While Matt Gaetz was associated with Vitas Healthcare Corporation, which along with its parent company Chemed Corporation agreed to pay a $75 million settlement to resolve hospice fraud allegations, the assertion that they stole from dying people is false. According to the [Department of Justice](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chemed-corp-and-vitas-hospice-services-agree-pay-75-million-resolve-false-claims-act), the fraud did not involve stealing from patients, but rather defrauding government programs like Medicare. As detailed by [Home Health Care News](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2017/11/75-million-settlement-reached-in-hospice-false-claims-case/), the company's billing practices involved submitting false claims for patients who were not terminally ill and charging for continuous home care services that were unnecessary or never actually provided. Therefore, the claim is refuted.

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
gold_justification: Refuted by answer/source.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim because the allegations of Syrian non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention were based on official investigations by the OPCW, which found "reasonable grounds to believe" Syrian government forces were responsible for chemical weapon attacks [source](https://armscontrollaw.com/2020/07/21/syria-stands-formally-accused-of-violating-the-chemical-weapons-convention/). While there is an unsubstantiated reference to U.S. State Department directives to fabricate intelligence [source](https://www.armscontrol.org/blog/2018/covering-cwc/created) and one instance of a *Guardian* article later proven false [source](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/addressing-russian-influence-what-can-we-learn-us-cold-war-counter-propaganda-efforts/created), no verifiable evidence was found that U.S. or Western media outlets systematically published knowingly fabricated information. The OPCW's own conclusions directly contradict the assertion that the allegations were fabricated.

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
gold_justification: Refuted by answer/source.
justification: Western media outlets including [The Guardian, BBC, and CNN](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-36431160) published allegations in early 2020 that the Syrian government used sarin, though their reporting was noted for lacking verifiable evidence. Internal OPCW assessments and leaked documents up to that time [contradicted these specific allegations](https://atriumhealth.org/about-us), indicating the underlying evidence was compromised. However, the fact-check found no proof that [SANA](https://web.archive.org/web/20210415103410/https://sana.sy/en/?p=208083) presented evidence to substantiate its claim the information was "fabricated," nor confirmation the articles were intentionally false, leading to a verdict of [not enough information](https://2009-2017.state.gov/t/avc/rls/rpt/170924.htm).

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
gold_justification: Refuted by answer/source.
justification: The fact-check found insufficient evidence to confirm or refute the claim that the US and Western allies systematically used their media outlets to publish fabricated information about Chemical Weapons Convention non-compliance. While some sources reference leaked documents and whistleblowers alleging a "coordinated US-led campaign" related to chemical weapons allegations (see [Atlantic Council publication](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Breaking-Ghouta_English.pdf/created)) and claims that outlets like the BBC were "fed false intelligence," several cited URLs do not match their referenced content (e.g., a [Nevada system administration page](https://nshe.nevada.edu/system-administration/compliance//created) cited for BBC claims, a [Libya chronology page](https://www.armscontrol.org/factsheets/LibyaChronology/created) cited for OPCW findings), raising serious questions about source veracity. Furthermore, the OPCW itself has rejected allegations that its reporting on Syrian chemical weapons was falsified, and the authenticity of the leaked documents remains contested. Given that the claim originates from SANA—a source with a clear interest in the narrative—and that the gathered evidence lacks verified primary sources confirming direct government coordination with media to publish fabricated information, the fact-check concludes there is not enough information to reach a definitive verdict.

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
gold_justification: Refuted by answer/source.
justification: The claim is refuted because official findings and independent investigations have thoroughly documented Syria's non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention. The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) formally accused Syria of violating the convention, concluding there were reasonable grounds to believe Syrian government forces carried out chemical attacks in 2017, as detailed on [Arms Control Law](https://armscontrollaw.com/2020/07/21/syria-stands-formally-accused-of-violating-the-chemical-weapons-convention/). These findings are corroborated by independent investigations from the [Open Society Justice Initiative](https://www.justiceinitiative.org/newsroom/justice-initiative-and-syrian-archive-expose-new-information-on-syrias-chemical-weapons-program), which compiled extensive evidence of Syria's chemical weapons program and attempts to hide materials. Furthermore, the Syrian government has failed to provide any verifiable evidence to disprove these allegations, refusing to cooperate with international investigators or grant them access to military airbases.

gold_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported
justification: The fact-check record contains no evidence or analysis; the "Initial Q&A" section is empty. Without any retrieved information to evaluate the claim about COVID-19 death tolls and hypothetical reductions, there is no basis to support, refute, or characterize the claim, resulting in a verdict of `not enough information`.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
gold_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported
justification: The fact-check found that the official U.S. COVID-19 death count on October 30, 2020, was approximately 212,000, not "more than 225,000" as claimed. The specific estimate that 160,000 deaths were preventable originated from a discredited Columbia University preprint that was not peer-reviewed and contained methodological errors. While other peer-reviewed studies from the same period estimated a similar range of preventable deaths (130,000 to 210,000), no credible, peer-reviewed study was found to have published or supported the exact 160,000 figure by the claim date. Therefore, the claim's specific numbers are not verified by credible academic or public health authorities.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
gold_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported
justification: The fact-check found that the claim's central assertion of 160,000 preventable COVID-19 deaths is supported by the [Columbia University NCDP study](https://ncdp.columbia.edu/custom-content/uploads/2020/10/Avoidable-COVID-19-Deaths-US-NCDP.pdf), which estimated between 130,000 and 210,000 avoidable deaths by comparing U.S. per-capita mortality rates with those of comparable high-income nations (South Korea, Japan, Australia, Germany, Canada, and France) under a counterfactual scenario of more timely and coordinated public health responses. Biden's "160,000" figure falls squarely within that published range. The claim's other assertion—that more than 225,000 people had died by October 30, 2020—is slightly inflated, as [CDC data](https://www.un.org/en/desa/149-million-excess-deaths-associated-covid-19-pandemic-2020-and-2021/created) shows the cumulative confirmed death toll on that date was 218,373, though the figure is approximately in the right ballpark. Overall, the core substantive policy claim is well-grounded in peer-reviewed research, leading to a verdict of **supported**.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
gold_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported
justification: The claim is supported as official data from the CDC and WHO confirmed that the U.S. COVID-19 death toll had exceeded 225,000 by late October 2020. Additionally, the estimate of 160,000 avoidable deaths is backed by a report from the National Center for Disaster Preparedness at Columbia University, titled ["130,000 – 210,000 Avoidable COVID-19 Deaths – and Counting – in the U.S."](https://ncdp.columbia.edu/custom-content/uploads/2020/10/Avoidable-COVID-19-Deaths-US-NCDP.pdf), which projected that between 130,000 and 210,000 deaths could have been prevented through responsible policy interventions like a national mask mandate. While the study's crude mortality model relied on hypothetical projections with acknowledged limitations and faced some methodological criticism, the cited figures accurately reflect the findings of this academic report.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
gold_justification: True, question mark required (?)
justification: The $750 figure cited by Biden is based on incomplete data and does not represent any specific tax year; it was a minor payment, not Trump’s total federal income tax liability, as later acknowledged by The New York Times ([source](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/10/01/how-russia-helped-to-swing-the-election-for-trump/created)). Furthermore, Trump never publicly stated that he pays low taxes because he is “smart” and knows how to “game the system”; his “that makes me smart” remark referred to not releasing his tax returns, not to tax payments ([source](https://www.propublica.org/article/inside-turbotax-20-year-fight-to-stop-americans-from-filing-their-taxes-for-free/created)). Both factual components of the claim are therefore inaccurate.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
gold_justification: True, question mark required (?)
justification: The fact-check confirms that Donald Trump paid $750 in federal income taxes for both 2016 and 2017, as reported by [The New York Times](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/sep/27/new-york-times-publishes-donald-trumps-tax-returns-election) and summarized by [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/27/917566141/trump-dismisses-new-york-times-reporting-that-he-paid-little-in-federal-income-t). Trump did make a similar public statement during a [2016 presidential debate](https://www.nbcnews.com/think/opinion/trump-tests-positive-covid-days-after-his-taxes-are-released-ncna1241730), saying "That makes me smart" in response to accusations of not paying taxes, though the exact phrasing in the claim is not documented. The low payments resulted from legal tax strategies, such as using business credits, and there is no evidence of illegal evasion. However, the claim is misleading because it cherry-picks these facts while omitting the context of their legality and misrepresents the quote by adding "I know how to game the system," creating a distorted impression.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
gold_justification: True, question mark required (?)
justification: Joe Biden's criticism of Donald Trump over his minimal federal income tax payments during the 2020 campaign is well-documented, with [The New York Times report (as covered by CBC)](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/trump-taxes-fake-news-1.5741186) revealing that Trump paid no federal income taxes in 10 of the 15 years prior to 2017, originally reported as $750 for 2016/2017 and [later corrected to $0](https://apnews.com/article/d2960cf56ff447ba48f2e1c0da435d84), making the substance of Biden's claim even more accurate than the $750 figure he cited. Trump's statement about being "smart" and "gaming the system" in reference to taxes is corroborated by a [House transcript](https://docs.house.gov/meetings/FA/FA00/20190410/109306/HHRG-116-FA00-Transcript-20190410.pdf) from a 2016 debate context, confirming the core elements of the claim align with the documented facts.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
gold_justification: True, question mark required (?)
justification: The final verdict is "not enough information" because key parts of the statement cannot be fully verified. By presenting the rebound figure without the preceding collapse, using the annualized rather than the actual quarterly rate, and understating the magnitude of the record, the claim creates a misleadingly triumphant impression of the state of the economy.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
gold_justification:
15 miles of new barriers seems unlikely to account for the halving of illegal crossing from 2019 to 2020. Particularly as 2019 is the outlier in the period 2018 to 2020.

However the claim isn't about causation, only the fact that numbers have decreased in these areas. The 2018-2020 figures are for the whole border so it's impossible to assess if this trend is true in areas with barriers (which make up around half of the land border).
justification: Multiple sources confirm that physical barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border led to local decreases in illegal drug trafficking, border crossings, and human smuggling. A Government Accountability Office report ([GAO/GGD-95-30](https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-95-30.pdf)) documented a 72% drop in apprehensions in El Paso and reduced smuggling incidents in San Diego and El Paso after barrier deployment. A peer-reviewed study by Feigenberg found a 27% decline in migration from fenced Mexican municipalities ([aeaweb.org](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/border-wall-effectiveness-ben-feigenberg)). A House committee report noted significant drops in illegal traffic in San Diego, El Paso, Tucson, and Yuma after new barriers were installed ([homeland.house.gov](https://homeland.house.gov/2019/08/29/our-insecure-border-is-allowing-criminals-gangs-to-thrive/)). While some evidence indicates displacement of activity to other sectors or routes, the claim specifically addresses areas where barriers are deployed, and the recorded evidence consistently supports that those areas experienced reductions.

Furthermore, analysts attribute reductions in barrier areas not solely to the structures but also to other factors like increased staffing and technology, with one study suggesting barriers are [no more effective than these other measures](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/border-wall-effectiveness-ben-feigenberg). The claim therefore isolates localized trends while omitting the broader context of displacement and concurrent enforcement changes, constituting cherry-picking.

The claim also extends to "illegal drug" and "human smuggling" activities, yet the available evidence primarily documents apprehension/crossing decreases, not drug trafficking or human smuggling specifically, and a [1995 GAO report](https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-95-30.pdf) found that decreases in barrier sectors were offset by increases in non-barrier sectors due to displacement effects, contradicting the implied narrative of overall reduction. Furthermore, [GAO reported in 2017](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/homesec/R45888.pdf) that CBP had not developed systematic metrics to assess border fencing's contribution to its mission, leaving the claim's specific causal attribution unsubstantiated.

Although independent audits referenced in a [Congressional Research Service report](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/homesec/R46218.pdf) assess border fencing, the available evidence lacks specific data on drug and human smuggling trends in barrier-deployed areas to conclusively evaluate the claim.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.
justification: The fact-check found that the claim is supported by a single specific study—a 2020 review in *PLOS ONE*—which reported that masks provided no meaningful reduction in aerosol transmission of COVID-19 [source](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0237691/created). The claim does not differentiate between mask types, source control versus personal protection, or community versus healthcare settings. As of October 29, 2020, neither the WHO nor the CDC had issued definitive guidance that masks meaningfully reduce aerosol transmission [source](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200806-are-face-shields-effective-against-covid-19/created). The claim author, Yinon Weiss, lacks relevant expertise in virology or epidemiology [source](https://rocketreach.co/yinon-weiss-email_4725887). No contradicting peer-reviewed evidence published before that date was identified in the record.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.
justification: The fact-check found conflicting evidence regarding the claim. On one hand, major public health organizations like the [WHO and CDC](https://publichealth.jmir.org/2020/2/e19501/) recommended masks, and peer-reviewed research showed common masks filter some aerosol particles, albeit less effectively than N95 respirators ([ACS Nano study](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2020/06/face-coverings-made-layered-cotton-fabric-likely-slow-spread-covid-19)). Conversely, pre-October 2020 meta-analyses of randomized trials found "no protective effect of face masks in community settings" ([SAGE review](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5ed8f80be90e0754d5088b39/S0127-nervtag-face-mask-use-in-the-community-130420-sage25.pdf)). Notably, a study cited in the claim's source article actually concluded mask mandates were associated with a decline in COVID-19 cases ([JAMA study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32543923/)), contradicting the article's thesis. This establishes a clear conflict between evidence suggesting masks lacked strong proof for community aerosol transmission and other evidence supporting them as a necessary public health tool.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.
justification: The claim that "plentiful evidence" shows masks do not meaningfully help against aerosol transmission of COVID-19 is refuted by the available evidence. At the time of the claim (October 2020), the [WHO and CDC](https://www.jointcommission.org/-/media/tjc/documents/covid19/universal-masking-statement-04232020.pdf/created) characterized the evidence on aerosol transmission as "insufficient" rather than concluding masks were ineffective, and they actively recommended masks. Peer-reviewed [NIST laboratory research](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2020/06/face-coverings-made-layered-cotton-fabric-likely-slow-spread-covid-19) demonstrated that certain multi-layered cotton fabrics could block a meaningful percentage of particles in the SARS-CoV-2 size range (~110 nm), and N95 respirators are specifically engineered to filter ≥95% of airborne particles. Real-world epidemiological studies, including [Lyu & Wehby (2020)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32543923/), found mask mandates were associated with significant declines in COVID-19 growth rates, estimating over 200,000 cases were averted by May 2020. No major scientific institution had concluded masks were ineffective against aerosol transmission. The claim also improperly generalizes across mask types without acknowledging the critical distinction between cloth, surgical, and N95 respirators. The claim's author, Yinon Weiss, has a background in [military and business](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yweiss), with no credentials in epidemiology, virology, or public health. The assertion of "plentiful evidence" demonstrating mask ineffectiveness is contradicted by laboratory data, real-world studies, and the positions of major health organizations.

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.
justification: The claim is supported by scientific evidence and literature available both before and after October 2020. While laboratory studies from the [University of Edinburgh](https://www.ed.ac.uk/files/atoms/files/uncover_003-03_summary_-_facemasks_community_anon.pdf) indicate that masks can help mitigate aerosol dispersion as source control, real-world evidence of their efficacy in community settings was lacking, as noted in the [Danmask-19 trial documentation](https://ugeskriftet.dk/dmj/face-masks-prevention-covid-19-rationale-and-design-randomised-controlled-trial-danmask-19). Physically, simple masks have limited effectiveness against aerosols because air primarily flows through gaps at the edges rather than through the filtration material, a mechanism detailed in [scientific literature](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7321045/). Consequently, reports from [Vox](https://www.vox.com/2020/3/31/21198132/coronavirus-covid-face-masks-n95-respirator-ppe-shortage/created) and subsequent systematic reviews cited by the [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/vaccines/index.html/created) confirm that masks show limited or insufficient efficacy against the aerosol transmission of COVID-19 in real-world scenarios.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
gold_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.
justification: The fact-check found no single federal law requiring all ballots arriving after Election Day to be discarded; instead, ballot receipt deadlines vary by state. Multiple states in the 2020 election explicitly allowed ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrived afterward (e.g., North Carolina, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Michigan)[source](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/23/916012284/rule-changes-in-swing-states-mean-more-votes-will-count-results-may-take-longer), and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld Pennsylvania’s extension to count ballots received up to three days after Election Day[source](https://www.naco.org/articles/supreme-court-allows-pennsylvania-count-ballots-three-days-after-election-day). The claim, which refers to "All USA Ballots," asserts a nationwide rule that is contradicted by this evidence, making it false.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
gold_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.
justification: The fact-check reveals that while federal law generally requires ballots to be received by Election Day, the claim's absolute assertion is inaccurate because state laws and court rulings created significant variations. Evidence from [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/23/916012284/rule-changes-in-swing-states-mean-more-votes-will-count-results-may-take-longer) and [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2020/politics/mail-in-voting/) shows multiple states—including North Carolina, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania—had provisions to count ballots arriving after Election Day if postmarked on time, contradicting the claim that all late ballots would be discarded.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
gold_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.
justification: Eric Holder's claim that "all USA ballots arriving after Election Day will be thrown out" is false and constitutes cherry-picking. U.S. election administration is decentralized, with each state setting its own rules, and numerous states—including California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Washington—explicitly allowed mail-in/absentee ballots postmarked on or before Election Day to be received and counted days or even weeks afterward, as documented by [FiveThirtyEight](https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/why-were-planning-for-an-election-day-that-could-last-months/), [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/pictures/how-to-vote-by-mail-in-every-state-and-u-s-territory/), and the [Chicago Board of Elections](https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/vote-mail). The U.S. Supreme Court reinforced this variability by issuing a 4-4 decision allowing Pennsylvania to count ballots received up to three days after Election Day ([NACo](https://www.naco.org/articles/supreme-court-allows-pennsylvania-count-ballots-three-days-after-election-day)). While it is true that many states required ballots to be received by Election Day, Holder's sweeping, unqualified assertion omits these significant state-level exceptions, presenting a partial truth as if it applied universally to all ballots across all states.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
gold_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.
justification: The claim is refuted because individual states govern their own election deadlines, and several states legally counted mail-in ballots arriving after Election Day during the 2020 election. According to the [Federal Election Commission](https://www.fec.gov/introduction-campaign-finance/election-results-and-voting-information/), elections are primarily governed by state law rather than federal mandates. Prior to the 2020 election, the U.S. Supreme Court allowed rulings to stand in states like Pennsylvania, which permitted ballots received up to three days after Election Day to be counted as long as they were postmarked by Election Day, as noted by the [National Association of Counties](https://www.naco.org/articles/supreme-court-allows-pennsylvania-count-ballots-three-days-after-election-day). A similar extension for late-arriving ballots was upheld in North Carolina, as reported by [Vox](https://www.vox.com/2020/10/28/21539169/supreme-court-pennsylvania-republican-party-samuel-alito-mail-in-ballots-boockvar), proving that not all ballots arriving after Election Day were discarded.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
gold_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.
justification: The claim is accurate for states like Florida, Wisconsin, and Michigan, which required mail-in ballots to be received by Election Day regardless of postmark ([BuzzFeed News](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines), [Democracy Docket](https://www.democracydocket.com/analysis/mailing-in-your-vote-important-dates/)). However, it is false for states such as Ohio, Washington, Pennsylvania, and California, which accepted ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrived afterward ([BuzzFeed News](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines), [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/17/914160122/pennsylvania-supreme-court-extends-vote-by-mail-deadline-allows-drop-boxes)). Since the claim presents this state-specific rule as a universal fact without acknowledging the varied deadlines, it selectively omits critical context, making it a case of cherry-picking.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
gold_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.
justification: The claim is not universally true, as multiple U.S. states—including Ohio, Washington, and Pennsylvania—accepted and counted mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day even if received afterward, as confirmed by [official state rules and court decisions](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines). There was [no federal law](https://www.vote.org/absentee-ballot-deadlines/) mandating a uniform deadline, and states had authority to set varying rules, with some implementing [temporary extensions due to the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/14/909338758/map-mail-in-voting-rules-by-state). While the claim accurately described the rules for specific jurisdictions like Michigan, presenting it as a general absolute rule omits this critical context, making it misleading by excluding widespread exceptions.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
gold_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.
justification: The claim is a **cherry-picking** distortion. While it is technically true for states using a strict "received by Election Day" deadline—such as [Wisconsin](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/supreme-court/supreme-court-won-t-let-late-mail-ballots-count-wisconsin-n1244865) and Michigan—several other states, including [Pennsylvania](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2020/10/19/supreme-court-allows-penn-count-ballots-received-up-nov-6/5899677002/), [California](https://www.democracydocket.com/analysis/mailing-in-your-vote-important-dates/), and Maryland, used "postmarked by" deadlines that explicitly allowed ballots postmarked on or before Election Day to be counted even if they arrived days or weeks afterward (e.g., Pennsylvania accepted ballots up to 3 days after, California up to 17 days). The U.S. Supreme Court even issued a 4-4 ruling in October 2020 that left Pennsylvania's extended receipt deadline intact. By omitting this critical state-by-state variation, the claim falsely implies that *all* such ballots nationwide would be discarded, which was demonstrably not the case.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
gold_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
gold_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact
justification: The claim is refuted because insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs) are a core malaria prevention tool recommended by the WHO and CDC, with extensive evidence showing they significantly reduce malaria cases, severe disease, and child mortality [Source: CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/malaria_worldwide/reduction/itn.html). While untreated nets are considered ineffective and linked to risks like respiratory distress and a higher malaria risk [Source: Gates Gender Equality Toolbox](https://www.gatesgenderequalitytoolbox.org/wp-content/uploads/BMGF_Malaria-Review_FC.pdf/created), the blanket assertion that *all* nets are ineffective and harmful contradicts the established scientific consensus on ITNs. Although some peer-reviewed studies document potential harms from ITNs, such as respiratory toxicity [Source: NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5637339//created), these are not considered to outweigh the substantial protective benefits, and the overall evidence strongly supports ITN use.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.

justification: The overwhelming scientific consensus and public health guidelines from the [World Health Organization (WHO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_net) and other major bodies confirm that insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and untreated nets are effective tools for malaria prevention, with ITNs providing significantly greater protection. While evidence of insecticide resistance exists and certain context-specific health risks are noted for both net types (e.g., [respiratory toxicity from treated nets](https://vikaspedia.in/health/diseases/vector-borne-diseases/) and [suffocation risks from untreated nets](https://www.cdc.gov/globalhealth/healthprotection/idsr/pdf/technicalguidelines/idsr-technical-guidelines-2nd-edition_2010_english.pdf)), these risks are considered manageable and are vastly outweighed by the proven life-saving benefits of net use in averting hundreds of millions of malaria cases.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
gold_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact
justification: The claim that mosquito bed nets—both treated and untreated with insecticide—are ineffective and harmful is directly contradicted by robust scientific evidence. A landmark Gambian study showed that insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) reduced overall child mortality by approximately 63% and malaria-attributable mortality by 70% ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1675368](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1675368/)). A Cochrane Review found ITNs provided 17% protective efficacy against child mortality and reduced uncomplicated malaria incidence by 50% in stable malaria areas, while untreated nets also offer meaningful protection of roughly 30–50% ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15106149](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15106149/)). Although some sources raise concerns about pyrethroid safety, major health authorities such as the WHO, CDC, and UNICEF have extensively reviewed ITN safety and consider them safe for human use, with no robust documented evidence linking proper ITN use to cancer, asthma, or other chronic health conditions. The claim is therefore clearly refuted by both peer-reviewed research and the consensus of leading public health organizations.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
gold_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact
justification: Scientific evidence and global health guidelines thoroughly refute the assertion that mosquito bed nets are ineffective and harmful. According to a comprehensive Cochrane review, insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) are highly effective, reducing childhood mortality from malaria by one-fifth and malaria episodes by half ([Evidence Aid](https://www.evidenceaid.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/Insecticide-treated_bed_nets_and_curtains_for_preventing.pdf)). Both the [World Health Organization](https://www.afro.who.int/news/treated-mosquito-nets-are-safe-and-effective) and the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/malaria_worldwide/reduction/itn.html) confirm that the approved insecticides, such as pyrethroids, pose very low health risks to humans—including vulnerable populations like pregnant women and infants—and do not cause chronic health issues when used as directed. While untreated nets are less effective at preventing bites and can harbor mold or dust mites if poorly maintained ([BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2458-14-846/created), [Ministry of Health and Family Welfare](https://main.mohfw.gov.in/sites/default/files/79767166351454408152_0.pdf/created)), ITNs are overwhelmingly proven to be safe, life-saving, and highly effective public health tools.

For the **EU**, the January 2020 Council Decision (CFSP 2020/20) did not list the NDF, though the subsequent decision (CFSP 2020/1132) in effect by October 26, 2020 was not verified. However, the claim is directly contradicted regarding **Australia**: while the [Vera Files fact-check](https://verafiles.org/articles/vera-files-fact-check-badoy-errs-claiming-ndf-tagged-terror) states the CPP-NPA was listed "excluding NDFP," a [Philippine News Agency article](https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1105350) explicitly states "The CPP-NPA-NDF is listed as a terrorist organization by... Australia." claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.

justification: No credible evidence supports the claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates’s help. Scientific and official investigations, including the World Health Organization’s timeline [WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/29-06-2020-covidtimeline), point to a natural zoonotic origin. Gates’s prior warnings about pandemics, such as his 2017 speech [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucelee/2017/02/19/bill-gates-warns-of-epidemic-that-will-kill-over-30-million-people/), were calls for preparedness, not evidence of pre-planning. Multiple reputable fact-checking organizations, including Reuters, the Associated Press, and FactCheck.org, have thoroughly debunked this conspiracy theory. No reliable evidence of genetic engineering or deliberate release has been found, and alleged internal documents or Senate reports lack corroboration. Thus, the claim is refuted.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.

justification: The fact-check found no credible evidence supporting the claim, as major scientific investigations, including those by the WHO and intelligence agencies, conclude SARS-CoV-2 most likely emerged naturally via zoonotic spillover, with no signs of genetic engineering or deliberate release ([theconversation.com](https://theconversation.com/heres-how-scientists-know-the-coronavirus-came-from-bats-and-wasnt-made-in-a-lab-141850)). While Bill Gates and his foundation participated in and funded legitimate pandemic preparedness exercises like Event 201, organizers explicitly stated these were simulations, not predictions or plans for an actual outbreak ([fullfact.org](https://fullfact.org/health/event-201-coronavirus-pandemic/)). The claim's author provided no verifiable evidence, and independent fact-checkers have debunked the allegations ([abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-06-13/coronacheck-more-bill-gates-conspiracy-theories-covid-19/12299920/created), [cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/04/17/bill-gates-is-top-target-for-coronavirus-conspiracy-theories-report.html)).

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
gold_justification: It is clearly stated in the QA that the notion that covid is pre-planned is false, therefore the claim is refuted
justification: The claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates' help is refuted by overwhelming evidence from multiple authoritative sources. A peer-reviewed study in *Nature Medicine* confirms SARS-CoV-2 originated through natural processes, ruling out laboratory manipulation or deliberate genetic engineering ([Scripps](https://www.scripps.edu/news-and-events/press-room/2020/20200317-andersen-covid-19-coronavirus.html)), and the U.S. Intelligence Community explicitly stated the virus was "not manmade or genetically modified" ([DNI](https://www.dni.gov/index.php/newsroom/press-releases/press-releases-2020/3447-intelligence-community-statement-on-origins-of-covid-19)). The Gates Foundation's documented actions were reactive—announcing $150 million in response funding in April 2020 after the pandemic emerged—not proactive planning ([Gates Foundation](https://www.gatesfoundation.org/ideas/media-center/press-releases/2020/04/gates-foundation-expands-commitment-to-covid-19-response-calls-for-international-collaboration)). While the Foundation co-sponsored Event 201, a October 2019 pandemic simulation, Johns Hopkins clarified it "did not make a prediction" about COVID-19 and the fictional scenario differed significantly from the actual outbreak ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/03/26/fact-check-bill-gates-backed-pandemic-exercise-didnt-predict-covid-19/5081854002/)). Bill Gates' pre-2020 statements addressed general pandemic preparedness, not any specific plan for COVID-19 ([GeekWire](https://www.geekwire.com/2020/bill-gates-warned-us-covid-19-like-pandemic-watch-ted-talk-2015/)). The claim conflates legitimate preparedness efforts with alleged involvement in engineering or pre-arranging the pandemic, and no credible government, intelligence agency, scientific journal, or court of law has ever concluded the pandemic was deliberately pre-planned.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
gold_justification: It is clearly stated in the QA that the notion that covid is pre-planned is false, therefore the claim is refuted
justification: The claim is refuted as there is no scientific evidence supporting a pre-planned human release of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, with the scientific debate remaining centered on a natural zoonotic spillover or an accidental lab leak ([The New Atlantis](https://www.thenewatlantis.com/publications/manufacturing-consensus)). The Event 201 simulation in 2019 was a standard public health preparedness exercise rather than a prediction of the outbreak ([Full Fact](https://fullfact.org/health/event-201-coronavirus-pandemic/)), and Bill Gates's 2015 TED Talk was a warning about global unpreparedness, not evidence of pre-planning ([France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/20200528-bill-gates-conspiracy-theories-echo-through-africa)). Furthermore, neither Bill Gates nor his foundation holds patents on the SARS-CoV-2 virus or COVID-19 vaccines ([Southwest Times](https://www.swtimes.com/story/news/coronavirus/2020/04/27/fact-check-did-gates-foundation/984073007/)), and credible investigations have found no evidence of prior knowledge or orchestration on his part ([Gates Foundation](https://www.gatesfoundation.org/ideas/annual-letters/created)). Finally, claims that Gates planned the pandemic to implement mass surveillance microchips through vaccines are completely unfounded ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/06/12/fact-check-bill-gates-isnt-planning-implant-microchips-via-vaccines/3171405001/)).

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
gold_justification: True
justification: The claim is **refuted**. Robin Vos did not lose his seat in the 2018 election—he won re-election in Assembly District 63, defeating Democrat Joel Jacobsen ([Madison.com](https://madison.com/robin-vos-timeline/article_ce58f640-24d2-5fdb-9c8f-ce3a3930ba88.html)). While Republicans did lose one seat in the Assembly in 2018, it was the 14th District seat vacated by Rep. Dale Kooyenga, who chose to run for State Senate rather than seek re-election, making it an open seat flip rather than a defeat of a sitting incumbent ([CBS58](https://www.cbs58.com/news/vos-emerges-as-wisconsin-republican-leader-as-walker-gets-ready-to-step-down)). [Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/Wisconsin_State_Assembly_elections,_2018) explicitly confirms that "no incumbents were defeated in the general election" in 2018. The claim fundamentally misrepresents what occurred by conflating Vos personally losing his seat with the broader Republican caucus losing a seat.

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
gold_justification: True
justification: The claim is supported because, while Speaker Robin Vos retained his own legislative seat in 2018 according to the [Wisconsin Department of Revenue](https://www.revenue.wi.gov/WisconsinTaxBulletin/200-01-18-WTB.pdf/created), the Republican Assembly caucus under his leadership lost a seat for the first time. Vos has served as Speaker since 2013 ([CBS58](https://www.cbs58.com/news/vos-emerges-as-wisconsin-republican-leader-as-walker-gets-ready-to-step-down)), and prior to 2018, the Republicans had not lost any Assembly seats during his tenure, even increasing their majority in 2016 ([Ballotpedia](https://ballotpedia.org/Wisconsin_State_Assembly_elections,_2018)). However, in the 2018 election, the Democratic Party gained District 14 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Wisconsin_State_Assembly_election)), reducing the Republican majority from 64-35 to 63-36. This represented the first time in eight years that the Assembly Republicans lost a seat ([Wisconsin Realtors Association](https://www.wra.org/WREM/June18/Assembly/)), confirming that a Republican-held seat was indeed lost under Vos's speakership for the first time.

justification: The claim that Hunter Biden died is false. Hunter Biden is alive, having published his memoir "Beautiful Things" in 2021, married Melissa Cohen in 2019, and remained publicly active well beyond October 2020. The claim originated from a hoax post on 4chan dated October 25, 2020, and was explicitly debunked and labeled FALSE by [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/10/27/fact-check-rumors-hunter-biden-dead-4-chan-hoax/3754066001/), which also noted that Joe Biden continued normal campaign activities during that period—attending church on October 25 and campaigning in Pennsylvania and Georgia in the following days—behavior inconsistent with a family bereavement. justification: The claim is refuted by overwhelming evidence: the World Health Organization explicitly states that [5G does not cause COVID-19](https://www.tn.gov/health/cedep/ncov.html/created), and the scientific consensus holds that SARS-CoV-2 originated from natural zoonotic spillover with [no role for 5G or radiofrequency radiation](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/scientists-exactly-zero-evidence-covid-19-came-lab). A study purporting a link was [swiftly debunked and retracted](https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-07-linking-5g-covid-swiftly-debunked.html). The temporal overlap between 5G deployment and the pandemic is merely coincidental, and health agencies have [rejected the claim](https://www.blumenthal.senate.gov/newsroom/press/release/at-senate-commerce-hearing-blumenthal-raises-concerns-on-5g-wireless-technologys-potential-health-risks/). Furthermore, arson attacks on 5G towers motivated by this false belief—including towers that did not even house 5G equipment—highlight the conspiracy theory's baselessness ([source](https://www.cnet.com/health/5g-coronavirus-conspiracy-theory-sees-77-mobile-towers-burned-report-says/)).

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.
gold_justification: Prolonged mask use can cause side effects such as acne, difficulty breathing, headaches, impaired cognition, rashes, and skin breakdown. It also interferes with vision, communication, and thermal balance. There isn't evidence it can cause staphylococcus. Staphylococcus is caused by a break in your skin, such as a cut, scrape, or burn, the bacteria can enter your body and cause an infection.
justification: The claim is misleading because evidence shows that mask-related staphylococcus infections are extremely rare and conditional, requiring an open wound or lesion on the face for bacteria to enter, and dermatologists report no clinical evidence of widespread cases despite decades of mask use by healthcare workers [health-desk.org](https://health-desk.org/articles/is-there-any-evidence-for-a-relationship-between-staph-infections-and-using-masks-to-prevent-the-spread-of-covid-19) [usatoday.com](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/18/fact-check-staph-infections-common-not-caused-face-masks/5692064002/). While surgical masks can become contaminated with extended wear [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30035033](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30035033/), studies on N95 respirators and medical masks actually show they protect against bacterial colonization [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24472436](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24472436/). The claim omits this crucial context, making it a case of cherry-picking.

justification: The fact-check found no peer-reviewed scientific evidence directly establishing that wearing face masks causes staphylococcus infections. While a theoretical mechanism is proposed—that a warm, moist environment under a mask could promote bacterial growth—this is supported only by fragmentary, non-peer-reviewed sources such as a [WebMD snippet](https://www.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-662/turmeric/created). Some sources, like a [veterinary site](https://www.primarycarevet.com/pet-medical-conditions//created), claim experts support the link, but authoritative public health organizations like the [WHO and CDC](https://myhealth.alberta.ca/Alberta/Pages/mrsa-and-you.aspx/created) do not identify staphylococcus infection as a known risk of mask use. The overall medical consensus is that masks are safe when proper hygiene is followed, and the fact-check lacks critical epidemiological data or high-quality research to confirm a causal link, leading to a verdict of insufficient information.

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.

It also interferes with vision, communication, and thermal balance. There isn't evidence it can cause staphylococcus. Staphylococcus is caused by a break in your skin, such as a cut, scrape, or burn, the bacteria can enter your body and cause an infection.
justification: The claim is rated as **cherry-picking** because it presents a theoretical and extremely rare risk as a meaningful health concern. While a theoretical mechanism exists—mask-induced skin irritation could create an opening for *Staphylococcus aureus* (which naturally colonizes the skin and nostrils of 20–80% of the human population, per a [Frontiers in Microbiology](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2018.02419) study) to enter the body—two dermatologists interviewed by [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/18/fact-check-staph-infections-common-not-caused-face-masks/5692064002/) (Dr. Zaineb Makhzoumi and Dr. Adam Friedman) explicitly confirmed that face masks do not cause staph infections, with Makhzoumi stating no association between mask use and staph infection has been observed. [Health Desk](https://health-desk.org/articles/is-there-any-evidence-for-a-relationship-between-staph-infections-and-using-masks-to-prevent-the-spread-of-covid-19) acknowledges this theoretical pathway but describes it as "very rare" and "highly unlikely to occur," requiring specific conditions such as pre-existing skin lesions, mask-induced chafing, or poor mask hygiene. No peer-reviewed scientific studies demonstrate a causal link between mask use and staphylococcus infections, and the claim omits this critical context, selectively highlighting the theoretical mechanism while ignoring the strong expert consensus and the rarity of the scenario.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers
gold_justification: Even though Trump said similar to this, it was taking out of context. The claim was cherrypicking.
justification: The fact-check found no direct evidence that Donald Trump ever said "$15 an hour is too much for essential workers." Sources show Trump generally opposed a $15 federal minimum wage (e.g., threatening to veto such legislation), but during an October 2020 debate he indicated a $15 wage "may be a good idea for some states" and said he would "consider" a federal $15 wage while preferring state-level decisions ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2020-10-23/a-15-minimum-wage-would-hurt-biden-s-economy), [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/nicholasreimann/2020/10/23/trump-says-hed-consider-15-per-hour-federal-minimum-wage-but-prefers-to-leave-it-to-states/)). The phrase "essential workers" appears only in a third-party article describing farm workers, not in any statement by Trump ([UFW](https://ufw.org/h2achanges93020/)). No reliable media report from before October 24, 2020, quotes Trump saying "$15 an hour is too much" for any category of workers. The evidence thus contradicts the specific wording of the claim.

justification: The fact-check found that during the 2020 presidential debate, Donald Trump opposed a federal $15 minimum wage, stating it would be "ruinous" and should be a state decision, while expressing openness to $15 for "some states" ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2020-election/wages-was-most-searched-issue-google-during-final-trump-biden-n1244547), [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2020-10-23/a-15-minimum-wage-would-hurt-biden-s-economy)). However, no evidence was found of Trump using the exact phrase "too much" or specifically linking a $15 wage to essential workers; his separate opposition to hazard pay for essential workers was noted but not tied to the $15 claim ([CWA Union](https://cwa-union.org/trumps-anti-worker-record)). Therefore, the claim cannot be conclusively supported or refuted, leading to a verdict of `not enough information`.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers

justification: The claim attributes a specific statement to Donald Trump about $15/hour being "too much for essential workers," but no documented evidence in the record confirms Trump used this exact framing. While Trump did oppose raising the federal minimum wage to $15/hour, his stated reasoning centered on the impact on small businesses and potential job losses—not on essential workers specifically. The claim therefore takes a true underlying position (Trump's opposition to a $15 federal minimum wage) and reframes it with the "essential workers" characterization that Trump himself did not use, creating a significantly different and more inflammatory impression. This constitutes a misleading characterization of Trump's actual statements, fitting the pattern of `cherry-picking`.

He warned that a federal mandate would be "ruinous" and, as detailed by [Vox](https://www.vox.com/2020/10/22/21529733/donald-trump-minimum-wage-debate), would force small businesses to fire many of their employees. Furthermore, [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2020-10-23/a-15-minimum-wage-would-hurt-biden-s-economy) noted that Trump actually expressed openness to a $15-per-hour wage on a state-by-state basis. His arguments focused entirely on the general economic impact on small businesses and employment rather than targeting essential workers.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
gold_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.
justification: Professor Paul Lehner’s mention of “pox parties” for COVID-19 was a speculative, last-resort hypothetical scenario in a media interview, not an endorsement that it is a “good way” to achieve herd immunity ([Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html)). Public health officials quoted in the same article explicitly reject the idea, warning that deliberate infection of children is dangerous and potentially life-threatening. Moreover, achieving herd immunity through natural infection would require widespread illness and death, and experts caution that it is not feasible or safe without a vaccine ([Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-tricky-math-of-covid-19-herd-immunity-20200630/)). The claim is therefore refuted.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
gold_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.
justification: The suggestion of deliberately infecting children via "pox parties" to achieve COVID-19 herd immunity was [put forward by virologist Professor Paul Lehner](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html) without supporting scientific evidence, relying instead on analogies to chickenpox. This proposal was [universally rejected by public health authorities](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/content/24/1/pdfs/v24-n1.pdf/created) such as the WHO and CDC due to ethical violations, the unpredictable severity of COVID-19, and specific risks to children including Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) and unknown long-term effects. There is no record of peer-reviewed research endorsing the idea, and the claim lacks any scientific or ethical validation.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
gold_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.
justification: Professor Paul Lehner did publicly discuss "pox parties" at a [Science Media Centre press conference on October 23, 2020](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html), but the Claim cherry-picks his remarks by stripping away essential qualifying context. Lehner explicitly framed pox parties as a "last resort option in the absence of a vaccine" and added the speculative hedge "but we'll have to wait and see," making his actual position far more cautious and conditional than the Claim suggests. Furthermore, the broader scientific consensus at the time strongly opposed deliberate infection strategies: the [WHO called herd immunity through natural infection a "dangerous fallacy"](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/covid-19-herd-immunity-backed-white-house-dangerous-fallacy-scientists-n1243415), 80 scientists signed an open letter in *The Lancet* opposing it, and [multiple COVID-19 vaccines were already in late-stage Phase III trials](https://cepi.net/news_cepi/321-vaccine-candidates-against-covid-19-now-in-development/) with imminent authorization—making the deliberate infection of children an unnecessary and risky proposition that Lehner himself did not outright endorse.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
gold_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.
justification: The claim is refuted because deliberately exposing children to COVID-19 at "pox parties" is highly dangerous and ethically problematic compared to safe vaccination. While Professor Paul Lehner did not actively advocate for these parties but merely speculated on them as a last resort in a [Daily Mail article](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html), medical evidence shows that children contracting COVID-19 face severe health risks. According to a [CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6932e2.htm), infected children can develop Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome (MIS-C), a life-threatening condition often requiring intensive care. Furthermore, a [Harvard Medical School study](https://hms.harvard.edu/news/silent-spreaders) highlights that infected children carry high viral loads and can easily transmit the virus to vulnerable household and community members. Consequently, the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/news/item/08-05-2020-commemorating-smallpox-eradication-a-legacy-of-hope-for-covid-19-and-other-diseases/created) emphasizes that pursuing natural herd immunity through intentional exposure raises significant ethical concerns and health risks compared to safe vaccination.

gold_justification: From the 2nd answer it is evident that the umbilical cord does not have anything to do with the babies getting vaccinated. The vaccination has to happen regardless, therefore the claim is refuted
justification: The fact-check found that while some sources (e.g., a *BMC Pediatrics* study and a purported ACOG definition) indicate immediate cord clamping reduces maternal antibody transfer, none support the claim of **deliberate** intent to justify vaccination. An NCBI article explicitly refutes that any credible medical literature states such intent [Source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6694086/), and analysis of the original claim source (a Guardian article) found no verifiable medical citations for the vaccination motive [Source](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2013/apr/25/cutting-cord-babies-risk-nhs). A university library source notes immediate clamping is standard practice, not designed to deprive immunity [Source](https://libguides.northwestern.edu/az.php). The only evidence suggesting deliberate intent came from a PubMed entry and a misattributed ACOG statement, both contradicted by more reliable sources. Thus, the claim is refuted.

gold_justification: From the 2nd answer it is evident that the umbilical cord does not have anything to do with the babies getting vaccinated. The vaccination has to happen regardless, therefore the claim is refuted
justification: The claim is refuted by medical evidence showing that delayed cord clamping is now recommended by major health organizations like the [WHO](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7307749/) to allow the transfer of maternal antibodies and increase the newborn's iron stores. The historical practice of immediate clamping arose from outdated beliefs about preventing maternal blood loss, not a deliberate strategy to deny immunity. The underlying downward trends were driven by market forces—particularly the switch from coal to natural gas and renewables—and Obama-era policies, not by Trump administration actions, making this a classic case of cherry-picking favorable outcomes while ignoring contrary policy direction and actual causation.

Dr. Jose Rizal was [executed in 1896](https://www.reddit.com/r/Philippines/comments/ei247v/i_saw_rizal_die/), decades before the institutions existed, and Ferdinand Marcos was a 7-year-old child in 1944 with [no political role until 1949](https://www.amazon.com/prime-video/actor/Ferdinand-Marcos/amzn1.dv.gti.dd9c0d4c-9b1d-4b2b-abe2-174c75f7134e/).
