The World Bank and IMF were established at the [Bretton Woods Conference in 1944](https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/137956/WP14.pdf), in New Hampshire, USA, by 44 Allied nations, with the principal architects being [Harry Dexter White](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/international-bank-of-reconstruction-and-development.asp) (U.S. Treasury) and John Maynard Keynes (United Kingdom). Dr. Jose Rizal was [executed in 1896](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Day)—nearly 50 years before these institutions existed—making it impossible for him to have founded them. Ferdinand Marcos, [born in 1917](https://www.amazon.com/prime-video/actor/Ferdinand-Marcos/amzn1.dv.gti.dd9c0d4c-9b1d-4b2b-abe2-174c75f7134e/), was only 27 years old and had not yet entered politics in 1944, and did not become President of the Philippines until 1965, more than two decades after these institutions were founded. claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
gold_justification: The answer and credible source show that the amount of deaths increased so the claim is refuted.
justification: Senator Johnson's statement referred specifically to Wisconsin, yet by October 4, 2020, the state's seven-day average of COVID-19 deaths had already doubled from six to fourteen, and Wisconsin was described as "the nation's COVID-19 hot spot" with rapidly rising hospitalizations and cases ([source](https://evers.wi.gov/Documents/COVID19/EmO03-LimitingPublicGatherings.pdf)). Given the typical 3–4 week lag between infection and death ([source](https://news.utexas.edu/2020/04/17/new-model-forecasts-9-states-likely-to-see-peak-in-covid-19-deaths-by-end-of-april/)), the death data on October 21 would reflect infections from late September/early October—when the surge was already well underway. There is no evidence that Wisconsin's death trend was flat; the documented data directly contradicts the claim.

gold_justification: The answer and credible source show that the amount of deaths increased so the claim is refuted.
justification: CDC data from October 21, 2020, showed a plateau in the 7-day moving average of daily COVID-19 deaths in the United States, supporting the claim's description of deaths being "pretty flat" at that time. However, the term ["flattening the curve"](https://www.npr.org/2020/03/11/814603316/public-health-experts-encourage-social-distancing-to-flatten-the-curve-of-infect) typically refers to slowing infections to prevent healthcare system overload, not to describing death trends. The fact-check found no evidence of a scientific or public health consensus in October 2020 that a "flattened curve" of infections was the direct cause of the stable death rate, leaving the claim's causal reasoning unconfirmed.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.

justification: On October 21, 2020, the 7-day rolling average of U.S. COVID-19 deaths was indeed stable at approximately 700–800 per day, and multiple sources characterize the trend as having "plateaued" following the spring 2020 surge ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/coronavirus-in-wisconsin-covid-19-death-toll-hits-400-total-cases-top-10k/), [BMC Medicine](https://bmcmedicine.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12916-020-01791-8), [White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/)), directly supporting the assertion that deaths were "pretty flat" on that date. While broader context—notably rising cases, the typical lag between case and death increases, and the looming "third wave" that drove deaths sharply higher in November and December 2020 ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/in-depth/graphics/2020/03/10/us-coronavirus-map-tracking-united-states-outbreak/4945223002/))—suggests this plateau was temporary, the claim as stated about the current state of deaths on October 21, 2020, is consistent with the available evidence.

Public health documentation, such as that from the [New York State Department of Health](https://coronavirus.health.ny.gov/home/created), defines "flattening the curve" as implementing public health measures that reduce infection rates and lead to stable death rates. Additionally, [Michigan Medicine](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/flattening-curve-covid-19-what-does-it-mean-and-how-can-you-help/created) confirms that the steady death rates during this period demonstrated the success of implemented measures to flatten the curve and reduce transmission.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
gold_justification: Studys show the flu vaccine does not affect how susceptible some one is to covid-19 so based on this it would mean Donald Trump was not more susceptible.
justification: The claim is refuted by multiple lines of evidence. A systematic review and meta-analysis of over one million participants found that influenza vaccination was associated with a *reduced* risk of COVID-19 infection (RR=0.83) [source](https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov/resource/pt/covidwho-1889175), not an increased susceptibility. Adjusted analyses accounting for confounders like age and comorbidities showed no link between flu vaccination and higher COVID-19 incidence or severity [source](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-clinical-and-translational-science/article/safety-of-influenza-vaccine-during-covid19/C26A417046677E65D421AD33B3E6281F). No peer-reviewed study or major health organization supports a causal mechanism for increased susceptibility, and the theoretical concern about vaccine-induced immune enhancement was not substantiated for SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19

This was supported by expert consensus and guidance from public health agencies like the CDC, which emphasized the flu vaccine's importance during the pandemic. No credible scientific mechanism, official medical records, or peer-reviewed research linked President Trump's flu shots to his COVID-19 infection, with alternative explanations like exposure to infected individuals being supported.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
gold_justification: Studys show the flu vaccine does not affect how susceptible some one is to covid-19 so based on this it would mean Donald Trump was not more susceptible.
justification: There is no scientific evidence to support the assertion that receiving an influenza vaccine increases susceptibility to COVID-19. While Donald Trump received a flu vaccine prior to his October 2020 diagnosis, health organizations have established that "vaccine interference" does not apply to the seasonal flu shot and SARS-CoV-2, meaning the flu vaccine does not make individuals more vulnerable to other respiratory infections ([HSE Library](https://hselibrary.ie/does-the-flu-vaccine-increase-the-risk-of-contracting-covid-19/)). Additionally, a widely cited January 2020 study by Greg G. Wolff on military personnel did not examine or draw any conclusions regarding COVID-19 ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/flu-vaccine-covid-buttar/)). In fact, a peer-reviewed 2022 meta-analysis of over one million participants published in the *American Journal of Preventive Medicine* found that influenza vaccination is actually associated with a reduced risk of COVID-19 infection and severity ([Global Literature on Novel Coronavirus 2019](https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov/resource/pt/covidwho-1889175)). Consequently, infectious disease experts strongly recommend that high-risk individuals receive seasonal flu vaccines to protect against co-infection ([Mass General](https://giving.massgeneral.org/stories/covid-19-and-the-flu-what-you-need-to-know/)).

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
gold_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.
justification: The fact-check found that Nate McMurray, as Town Supervisor of Grand Island, **New York** (not Nebraska), voted with the Town Board to approve a 2020 budget that raised the property tax levy by 3.47% [source](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html), which increased taxes on homeowners. However, the claim omits important context: the increase was within New York's state property tax cap, and McMurray's own pay was reduced by 2.8% [same source]. Additionally, the claim misstates the location as Nebraska instead of New York [source](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/buffalo/politics/2018/01/10/nate-mcmurray-to-announce-candidacy-for-congress). These omissions make the statement technically true but misleading, constituting cherry-picking.

justification: The fact-check establishes that Nate McMurray served as Town Supervisor of Grand Island in [New York, not Nebraska](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/upshot/elections-poll-ny27-3.html). During his term, the [Town Board voted in November 2018](https://ecode360.com/documents/GR0053/public/466406368.pdf) to approve the 2020 budget, [raising the overall tax levy by 3.47%](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html), which was [justified](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html) as funding a one-time hydrant replacement project. However, the available documentation does not specify whether this levy increase was specifically applied to homeowners as a distinct class, leaving insufficient information to conclusively verify the claim's precise wording.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
gold_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.
justification: The claim contains a significant factual error: Nate McMurray served as Town Supervisor of Grand Island, **New York**, not Nebraska as stated by the claim author ([Spectrum News](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/buffalo/politics/2018/01/10/nate-mcmurray-to-announce-candidacy-for-congress)). While a Grand Island does exist in Nebraska ([Visit Grand Island](https://visitgrandisland.com/plan-a-trip/things-to-do/nature-wildlife.html)), it is a separate and unrelated municipality. Regarding the tax vote assertion, evidence confirms that during McMurray's tenure, the Grand Island Town Board approved budgets that raised taxes—notably the 2020 budget, which increased the overall property tax levy by 3.47%, the general fund tax rate by 2.2%, and the water district tax rate by 34% ([Buffalo News via Wayback Machine](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html)). However, the available sources do not specifically document McMurray's individual vote (yea or nay) on these measures, only attributing approval to "the Town Board" generally, and meeting minutes show the motions to adopt the budget were made by other council members ([ecode360](https://ecode360.com/documents/GR0053/public/466406368.pdf)). The claim is therefore misleading: the incorrect state misrepresents where McMurray served, and the specific assertion that he personally "voted to raise taxes" is not directly substantiated by the evidence, even though tax increases did occur during his tenure.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
gold_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.
justification: The claim is refuted because Nate McMurray never served as the Town Supervisor of Grand Island, Nebraska. According to [Politifact](https://www.politifact.com/personalities/nathan-mcmurray/), McMurray actually served as the Town Supervisor of Grand Island, New York. As documented by [Spectrum News](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/buffalo/politics/2018/01/10/nate-mcmurray-to-announce-candidacy-for-congress), Representative Chris Jacobs mistakenly named Nebraska instead of New York in his statement. Since McMurray never held public office in Nebraska, it is factually impossible for him to have voted to raise taxes in that capacity.

claim: Russia sent medical aid to the US, in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients.
gold_justification: Evidence finds that Russia did send medical equipment to the United States; however, the U.S. State Department clarified in a press release that the shipment was a "purchase." The JSS covers 67% of wages up to £2,100/month, but UC eligibility depends on income, savings, and other factors, meaning many workers—such as those with savings over £6,000 or higher earners—receive less than 80% [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147). Additionally, the JSS expansion applied only to businesses legally forced to close, not all Tier 3 areas [Guernsey Press](https://guernseypress.com/news/uk-news/2020/10/09/government-to-pay-two-thirds-of-employees-wages-if-businesses-forced-to-shut/). While Universal Credit could top up the JSS payment to at least 80% for some workers, eligibility depended on income, savings, and dependents — workers with £16,000 in savings would not qualify for any Universal Credit at all, and the Institute for Fiscal Studies calculated that a single person earning £11,000/year with no children would receive only 73% of their usual income, as confirmed by the [BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147). The DWP's confirmation of the 80% figure was explicitly limited to low-income workers receiving the full UC entitlement, meaning the claim cherry-picks the most favorable scenario while omitting crucial context about caps, savings thresholds, and the scheme's not-yet-active status.

Consequently, many workers would only receive the 67% JSS rate, and analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) demonstrated that even some who qualified for UC would only receive about 73% of their normal income ([BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147)). Additionally, claimants faced a five-week waiting period for their first UC payment ([Understanding Universal Credit](https://www.understandinguniversalcredit.gov.uk/new-to-universal-credit/how-and-when-youll-be-paid/)), and the JSS itself was ultimately postponed ([Sargent Disc](https://www.sargent-disc.com/2020/09/29/covid-19-job-support-scheme/)).

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
gold_justification: The 2nd Q&A pair point out that from 2019 there was no more penalty for having no health insurance in the US, whilst the claim was made in 2020.
justification: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) provided exemptions from the individual mandate penalty for those who could not afford coverage, such as when insurance costs exceeded 8.13% of household income ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-reform/issue-brief/the-cost-of-the-individual-mandate-penalty-for-the-remaining-uninsured/)). The penalty for an individual was never set at $10,000; the maximum for a single person was capped at the national average cost of a Bronze plan, and even for a family of five or more in 2015 it could reach $12,420 ([FAS](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R41331.pdf)). By the 2020 tax year, the penalty had been reduced to $0 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 ([Holland & Hart](https://www.hollandhart.com/2019-repeal-of-the-affordable-care-acts-individual-mandate-penalties)). Thus, the claim is contradicted on multiple grounds.

justification: The claim is refuted because it mischaracterizes how the ACA's individual mandate penalty worked. The $10,000 figure was a maximum cap (equal to the national average bronze plan premium), not a standard penalty applied to everyone; the penalty was actually calculated as the greater of a flat dollar amount (~$695 per adult) or 2.5% of household income above tax filing thresholds, meaning lower-income individuals who "couldn't afford" coverage would face penalties far below $10,000, if any ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-reform/issue-brief/how-many-of-the-uninsured-can-purchase-a-marketplace-plan-for-less-than-their-shared-responsibility-penalty/)). Furthermore, the ACA included hardship and affordability exemptions to protect people who genuinely could not afford coverage, and provided premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies to help lower-income individuals afford insurance ([CBPP](https://www.cbpp.org/research/health/improving-aca-subsidies-for-low-and-moderate-income-consumers-is-key-to-increasing)). Most critically, the federal individual mandate penalty was reduced to $0 effective January 1, 2019—over a year before the claim was made on October 20, 2020—through the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 ([Holland & Hart](https://www.hollandhart.com/2019-repeal-of-the-affordable-care-acts-individual-mandate-penalties)), making the claim factually impossible at the time it was posted.

Historically, the law provided [exemptions for low-income individuals](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/complying-coppa-frequently-asked-questions/created) who could not afford coverage. While penalties were calculated based on income and could theoretically exceed $10,000 for high earners ([HHS Guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/2012232553-jp-py21_basics_exam.pdf/created); [GovInfo](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CPRT-115SPRT28110/html/CPRT-115SPRT28110.htm/created)), they were capped at the national average cost of a Bronze-level health plan ([HealthInsurance.org](https://www.healthinsurance.org/glossary/individual-mandate/)). Furthermore, the IRS was legally prohibited from using standard enforcement methods like liens, levies, or criminal prosecution to collect unpaid mandate penalties ([Congressional Research Service](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R41331.pdf)).

claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.
gold_justification: The Q&A's only mention excess death due to covid and so no data for other causes such as the claimed 'lockdowns' so more evidence is needed.
justification: The fact-check found that in the US, excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 in 2020 were substantial—33% of ~225,530 excess deaths per a [JAMA study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2771761) and ~100,947 per the [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf). A [medRxiv study](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.26.20098434v1.full) directly documents a mechanism linking lockdowns to these deaths: a 43.8% reduction in acute medical admissions and more than double the risk of in-hospital death from delayed care for time-sensitive conditions like heart attacks. Other sources note that non-COVID excess deaths could reflect pandemic disruptions, including stay-at-home orders, but do not isolate lockdown effects from other pandemic factors. While no rigorous causal analysis separates lockdowns from broader pandemic impacts, the documented pathway via delayed medical care supports the claim that lockdowns were partly responsible. Thus, the claim is **supported**.

gold_justification: The Q&A's only mention excess death due to covid and so no data for other causes such as the claimed 'lockdowns' so more evidence is needed.
justification: Based on the fact-check record, the claim that lockdowns contributed to non-COVID-19 excess deaths is not definitively supported by available evidence. While [a CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf) confirmed significant excess deaths in 2020, with [about 26% not directly attributed to COVID-19](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/US-covid-deaths-may-be-underestimated-36-percent), the causes are complex. Research points to indirect factors like [delayed medical care due to pandemic-related fear](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6936a4.htm) and broader societal impacts such as economic hardship. Although some analyses, like [one in *PLOS ONE*](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0261759), model a link between lockdown-induced economic loss and increased mortality, and [a UK government report](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5f2c23b38fa8f57ac287c161/s0650-direct-indirect-impacts-covid-19-excess-deaths-morbidity-sage-48.pdf) suggests lockdowns could contribute to excess deaths, the evidence does not establish a direct, isolated causal relationship between specific lockdown measures and the observed deaths. The issue is contested, with lockdown effects difficult to disentangle from the pandemic's overall impact, leading to the final verdict of `not enough information`.

claim: In the US lockdowns are partly responsible for excess deaths not directly attributed to COVID-19 which were observed in 2020.

justification: The claim that US lockdowns are "partly responsible" for non-COVID-19 excess deaths in 2020 is not directly supported nor refuted by the available evidence. The CDC confirmed that approximately one-third of excess deaths from January through October 2020 were not attributed to COVID-19, with leading causes including heart disease, Alzheimer disease/dementia, and diabetes ([CDC MMWR](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf)), and acknowledged these deaths may be "indirectly related to the pandemic (e.g., because of disruptions in health care access or utilization)" or misclassified COVID-19 deaths. However, no source reviewed isolates or quantifies lockdowns as a distinct causal factor separate from broader pandemic effects. Instead, non-COVID-19 excess deaths are attributed to general pandemic-related factors such as fear of seeking medical care ([Penn Today](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/US-covid-deaths-may-be-underestimated-36-percent)), economic and mental health impacts, and healthcare disruptions. Additionally, a [PLOS ONE study](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0261759) defined US lockdown measures but did not link them to non-COVID-19 excess mortality. The CDC has not explicitly attributed any portion of non-COVID-19 excess deaths to lockdown policies, and the claim's specific causal assertion lacks direct evidentiary support in the reviewed sources.

gold_justification: The Q&A's only mention excess death due to covid and so no data for other causes such as the claimed 'lockdowns' so more evidence is needed.
justification: During 2020, the United States recorded approximately 100,000 excess deaths that were not officially attributed to COVID-19, according to a [CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/pdfs/mm6942e2-H.pdf). While a [study](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7576405/) identified significant increases in deaths from non-COVID causes like heart disease and dementia, it remains unclear whether these were due to undiagnosed COVID-19 infections or indirect pandemic disruptions. Although a [CDC study on emergency department visits](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6925e2.htm) suggested that avoided care might explain some excess mortality, it lacked direct empirical evidence linking this to lockdown policies. Additionally, a [PLoS ONE study](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0261759) modeled potential deaths from economic distress but relied on historical correlations rather than direct causal proof. Because existing research cannot isolate the specific impacts of lockdown policies from other confounding pandemic factors, there is not enough information to definitively confirm or deny their role in these excess deaths.

justification: The 372,000 figure originates from a [ProPublica/Philadelphia Inquirer investigation](https://www.propublica.org/article/pennsylvanias-rejection-of-372-000-ballot-applications-bewilders-voters-and-strains-election-staff) and is factually accurate, but the claim materially misrepresents what it represents: these were rejected ballot **applications** (requests), not rejected mail-in ballots themselves. Over 90% of the rejections—approximately 336,000—were duplicate applications from voters who had unknowingly checked a box to receive ballots for both the primary and general election, and [those voters could still receive a ballot or vote in person on Election Day](https://www.inquirer.com/politics/election/pennsylvania-mail-ballot-rejections-duplicate-applications-20201016.html), meaning no voters were ultimately disenfranchised. The headline's omission of this critical context—particularly that these were applications rather than ballots, and that the vast majority were harmless duplicates—creates a significantly more alarming impression than what actually occurred, making this a case of cherry-picking and misleading framing.

justification: Pennsylvania election officials did not reject 372,000 cast mail-in ballots; rather, this figure represents rejected mail-in ballot *applications*, the vast majority of which were duplicates. This surge in duplicate applications caused significant voter confusion, forcing county election offices to hire temporary staff, work seven days a week, and expand call center capacity to handle the high volume of inquiries.
